title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
authors: Lluís Arola-Fernández, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length.

title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks? We study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. As sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds. Learning a generalizing solution is really just underfitting the memorizing solution; feature learning is inessential to ICL. Transformers empirically trained to do ICL memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts.

title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval
authors: Dohoon Kim, Junho Park, Hyunwoong Bae, Seyoon Kim, Taesup Moon
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. We propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by +1.28 to +1.56 pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.

title: A Common Recognition Architecture Across Memory Scales
authors: C. Zhao, A. Kim, S. Horwitz, T. Adekoya, E. K. Vogel
abstract: Recognition decisions occur across memory episodes that vary vastly in scale, from compact single-item episodes to extended experiences involving hundreds of items. We recorded EEG while participants performed a recognition memory task across set sizes ranging from 1 to 128 items (spanning 2 to 256 recognition judgments). Classic electrophysiological signatures of recognition, including frontal and parietal old/new effects, persisted continuously across set sizes. Multivariate neural classifiers trained on small memory scales generalized robustly across set sizes. Rather than revealing distinct neural formats, increasing memory scale produced systematic, continuous shifts in the timing and strength of a shared recognition response: signals emerged progressively later and weaker at larger memory scales. Individual difference analyses revealed that this common recognition format tracks working-memory capacity at smaller scales and long-term memory performance at larger scales.

title: Disentanglement of persistent and dynamic neural substrates of working memory
authors: A. Abbasi, A. Nanda, W. Dang, B. Singh, Z. Wang, C. Constantinidis, M. Rubinov
abstract: Competing theories of working memory have alternatively emphasized persistent and dynamic substrates. We directly tested these theories by computationally isolating the contributions of persistent and dynamic activity. We analyzed neuronal population activity recordings in macaques doing match/non-match working memory tasks, extracted signatures of persistent and dynamic activity through cue-specific temporal means, temporal principal components, and correlations of activity patterns across task epochs, then generated synthetic data constrained by these signatures and decoded cue stimuli separately from persistent and non-persistent neurons. We could decode stimuli at empirical or above-chance levels across all tasks only from persistent neurons, but only after constraining correlations of activity patterns across epochs.

title: Hippocampal CA2 modulates trace fear conditioning through circuit-specific tuning of CA1 activity
authors: Thomas E. Bassett, Hui Zhang, Zorica Petrovic, et al. (Jelena Radulovic)
abstract: Forming associations between temporally separated events depends on pathways linking CA1, subiculum and entorhinal cortex. Using trace fear conditioning (TFC), in which mice learn to associate a tone and shock separated by a temporal gap, we found that chronic blockade of dorsal CA2 output reduced cue-associated freezing without comparable effects following delay fear conditioning or during contextual fear recall. Acute inhibition of dCA2 to dCA1 projections during conditioning or recall increased cue-test freezing, whereas inhibition of dCA2 to dSUB projections produced no behavioral effect. Fiber photometry showed dCA2 to dCA1 calcium activity exhibited tone-onset modulation during conditioning and late-trace modulation near the time at which shock had occurred. Acute CA2 inhibition during conditioning was associated with persistent tone-onset CA1 modulation during subsequent drug-free recall.

title: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction
authors: Hao Gu, Xintong Yang, Zhiwei Li, et al. (Sirui Han)
abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A learnable gate inside the normalizing softmax suppresses one entry and hands its mass to the others; that same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op. Both obstacles are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate's reach and making the dense model's predictions its target. Capacity is never the missing ingredient. What eviction unavoidably discards is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it. At 75% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.

title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
authors: Simone Betteti, Matteo Martin, Morten Gram Pedersen, Sandro Zampieri, Giacomo Baggio
abstract: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points.

title: Thermodynamics of Forgetting in a Bounded Hopfield Network
abstract: A memory that keeps learning must also forget. Parisi showed in 1986 that bounding the synaptic strength cures the Hopfield network's catastrophic confusion, since clipping the couplings gradually erases the oldest memories. We provide a thermodynamic description of the Hopfield-Parisi model. Starting from the learning rule, we show the network is equivalent to a Hopfield model whose patterns are weighted according to their age, superimposed on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, both governed by the synaptic bound: a larger bound makes the memory longer but also noisier. We rederive the replica-symmetric equations through Guerra's interpolation and solve them at finite temperature, obtaining the phase diagram together with the memory horizon, the largest age at which a pattern can still be retrieved. The solution shows that forgetting acts on the signal alone, the noise being the same for patterns of every age, and that the horizon is maximal at an intermediate bound essentially insensitive to temperature. Monte Carlo simulations support these predictions.

title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI
authors: Deniz Kumral, Antonia Lenders, Monika Schönauer
abstract: Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest, localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus. Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions emerging as early as ~7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ~35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes.

title: The behaviour bends, the code holds: working-memory category information in the multiple-demand network across graded interruption
abstract: We examined how the multiple-demand (MD) network represents a memorandum when an unrelated task interrupts maintenance. Participants memorised an image of a tool or animal and, during the delay, performed a digit task whose difficulty was parametrically varied (passive, easy, hard). Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, we decoded the maintained category from 13 MD regions and early visual cortex. Behaviourally, interruption reduced recall accuracy, while the most demanding interrupter slowed responses. Neurally, category information was present during the delay, most strongly in visual cortex and bilateral intraparietal sulcus, and was unaffected by task engagement, consistently across decoding accuracy and cross-validated Mahalanobis distance, with Bayesian evidence supporting the null effect. Increasing the demand of the active interrupter produced a modest, network-wide reduction in crossnobis distance that was not detectable in decoding accuracy.

title: Enhancing the Suppression of Unwanted Memories During NREM Sleep
authors: Ruyue Xie, Zhiyuan Guo, Haobo Zhang, et al. (Xu Lei)
abstract: We combined the Think/No-Think paradigm with targeted memory reactivation to investigate whether reactivating suppression processes during sleep influences later memory. Participants learned cue-associate word pairs, then were presented with trials each exposing a cue word preceded by an auditory instruction to retrieve or suppress the target word. During NREM sleep we unobtrusively re-presented the auditory tone signaling the instruction to suppress retrieval. Cueing people to suppress significantly enhanced suppression-induced forgetting on a later post-sleep test compared with pairs not cued during sleep. EEG analyses revealed that reactivation of suppression instructions increased theta power and reduced coupling strength between spindles and the slow-osculation up-states. Only reduced SO up-state-spindle coupling predicted poorer later memory retrieval for suppressed pairs.

title: Human and Machine Annotations Predict Brain Responses to Naturalistic Movies Across Development
authors: Yiran Huang, Zeyong Zhang, Rounak Rahman, Bharat Biswal, Xin Di, Mengjia Xu
abstract: We investigated whether multimodal large language models can provide scalable socio-affective and semantic annotations for naturalistic fMRI. We compared MLLM-generated theory-of-mind and valence ratings with human ratings and with regional BOLD responses across three animated movies. For two movies, we combined machine-derived visual features, natural-language scene descriptions, and socio-affective ratings in an ROI-wise encoding model of fMRI data from 66 participants aged 5-22 years. MLLM ratings partially tracked human judgments, but their neural correspondence differed by construct and model: ToM showed the most consistent human-machine overlap in visual cortex, whereas valence correspondence was largely movie dependent. Visual features yielded the strongest and most widespread prediction, whereas scene descriptions were more spatially selective, concentrated in dorsal-attention and visual regions and extending into right lateral temporal cortex.

title: BrainBind: Bridging Synchronized EEG and fMRI through Long-Form Naturalistic Video Representations
authors: Shixiao Wang, Rining Wu, Jian K. Liu
abstract: We study the synchronized case: EEG and fMRI are recorded during the same long-form naturalistic viewing, giving a shared stimulus but also recurring narrative context and many semantically similar candidates. We present BrainBind, a framework that maps synchronized EEG and fMRI into frozen long-form video embedding spaces and treats those spaces as common visual-semantic references, not literal neural codes. On CineBrain, a five-seed Recall@K 2x4 matrix across two video anchors and four system configurations shows distinct retrieval profiles. With Omni, fMRI organizes the full candidate list most strongly (MRR = 23.82, nDCG@10 = 25.31), while Joint-Dual gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%). The complementary episode-disjoint evaluation quantifies the contribution of repeated stimulus identity and narrative context to the random split. The code is available at https://github.com/Forainest789/Brainbind.

title: Archival and palaeoenvironmental documentation of extreme climate events reveals generational amnesia in collective memory
authors: Shuang Song, Bo Hu, David Max Findley, et al. (Patrick Roberts)
abstract: Collective memory shapes how societies respond to extreme climate events, yet long-term evidence on how the collective memory of such events becomes perceptually biased over time is lacking. We utilise four centuries (1470-1900) of climatic archives from northern China, along with tree-ring-based hydroclimate reconstructions validated against instrumental Wet/Dry Index observations (1901-2000). Historical records reveal systematic, non-random mismatches, where severity assessments are often biased toward recent experience rather than absolute climatic anomalies. Correlations between historical and natural records increase when the natural series is re-standardised using 20-40-year sliding windows, reflecting a generational offset. A heuristic agent-based model reproduces this pattern, suggesting that generational amnesia is sufficient to explain the offsets in perception of environmental change.
